q: A 34-year-old man presents with a 10-day history of fever, sore throat, myalgia and a maculopapular rash. He had unprotected receptive anal intercourse with a new male partner 3 weeks ago. On examination he has generalised lymphadenopathy and shallow oral ulcers. A fourth-generation HIV antigen/antibody combination assay is positive but the confirmatory HIV-1/2 antibody differentiation immunoassay is indeterminate. Bloods: lymphocytes 0.9 x10^9/L, ALT 78 U/L. Which single investigation is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis of acute HIV infection at this stage?
options: Repeat HIV antibody differentiation immunoassay in 12 weeks
HIV-1 RNA quantification (viral load) by PCR
explain: This is acute (primary) HIV seroconversion. 🦠 In the earliest window the combined Ag/Ab assay turns positive (driven by p24 antigen) before a mature antibody response develops, so the confirmatory antibody differentiation immunoassay is often negative or indeterminate. The definitive test to resolve this discordance and confirm acute infection is HIV-1 RNA (viral load) by PCR, which is detectable ~10 days after infection and is typically very high (>100,000 copies/mL) in seroconversion.\n\nBHIVA/US algorithms specify that a reactive combined assay with a negative/indeterminate differentiation assay should be resolved with an HIV-1 RNA test. Waiting 12 weeks delays treatment and transmission-prevention. CD4 count assesses immune status but does not confirm infection. p24 alone is less sensitive than the combined workflow already performed. HIV-2 Western blot is not indicated given the epidemiology and would not resolve an early HIV-1 diagnosis.

The definitive test to resolve this discordance and confirm acute infection is HIV-1 RNA (viral load) by PCR, which is detectable ~10 days after infection and is typically very high (>100,000 copies/mL) in seroconversion.\n\nBHIVA/US algorithms specify that a reactive combined assay with a negative/indeterminate differentiation assay should be resolved with an HIV-1 RNA test. Waiting 12 weeks delays treatment and transmission-prevention. CD4 count assesses immune status but does not confirm infection. p24 alone is less sensitive than the combined workflow already performed. HIV-2 Western blot is not indicated given the epidemiology and would not resolve an early HIV-1 diagnosis.

A.html: Repeating antibody testing in 12 weeks unnecessarily delays diagnosis, treatment and partner protection. In acute infection antibodies are still evolving, so a repeat differentiation assay may remain indeterminate for weeks while RNA is already strongly positive.
A.text: Repeating antibody testing in 12 weeks unnecessarily delays diagnosis, treatment and partner protection. In acute infection antibodies are still evolving, so a repeat differentiation assay may remain indeterminate for weeks while RNA is already strongly positive.

B.html: CD4 count stratifies immunosuppression and guides opportunistic infection prophylaxis, but it is neither sensitive nor specific for confirming HIV infection. A transiently low CD4 can occur in many acute viral illnesses.
B.text: CD4 count stratifies immunosuppression and guides opportunistic infection prophylaxis, but it is neither sensitive nor specific for confirming HIV infection. A transiently low CD4 can occur in many acute viral illnesses.

C.html: HIV-1 RNA PCR is detectable ~10 days post-infection and is markedly elevated during seroconversion, resolving the discordant serology. It is the recommended confirmatory step when a combined assay is reactive but the antibody differentiation assay is indeterminate.
C.text: HIV-1 RNA PCR is detectable ~10 days post-infection and is markedly elevated during seroconversion, resolving the discordant serology. It is the recommended confirmatory step when a combined assay is reactive but the antibody differentiation assay is indeterminate.

D.html: p24 antigen is already captured within the fourth-generation combined assay. Repeating it in isolation adds nothing and is less reliable than RNA quantification for confirming very early infection.
D.text: p24 antigen is already captured within the fourth-generation combined assay. Repeating it in isolation adds nothing and is less reliable than RNA quantification for confirming very early infection.

E.html: HIV-2 is rare outside West Africa and the clinical/epidemiological picture points to HIV-1. A Western blot would not detect early HIV-1 antibodies and is not part of the modern confirmatory algorithm.

q: A 41-year-old woman with untreated HIV presents with 3 weeks of progressive exertional dyspnoea and a dry cough. Oxygen saturation is 91% on air, falling to 84% after climbing stairs. Chest examination is unremarkable. CD4 count is 90 cells/mm3. Chest radiograph shows bilateral perihilar interstitial infiltrates. Serum lactate dehydrogenase is elevated. Induced sputum immunofluorescence confirms the diagnosis. In addition to high-dose co-trimoxazole, which single additional therapy is most strongly indicated?
options: Immediate initiation of antiretroviral therapy that day
explain: This is Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) with hypoxia and exertional desaturation. 🫁 The key management point is that adjunctive corticosteroids are indicated in moderate-to-severe PCP, defined as PaO2 <9.3 kPa on air or an A-a gradient >4.7 kPa (SaO2 here is 91% resting, desaturating markedly). Steroids blunt the inflammatory surge triggered by dying organisms during the first days of anti-pneumocystis therapy, reducing respiratory deterioration and mortality.\n\nFirst-line antimicrobial therapy remains high-dose co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) for 21 days. Nebulised pentamidine is an inferior alternative reserved for mild disease/intolerance, not monotherapy here. Ganciclovir treats CMV, not Pneumocystis. Caspofungin has poor single-agent efficacy. ART is essential but is usually started ~2 weeks after beginning PCP treatment to reduce immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome risk, so 'that day' is not the strongest immediate answer.

Steroids blunt the inflammatory surge triggered by dying organisms during the first days of anti-pneumocystis therapy, reducing respiratory deterioration and mortality.\n\nFirst-line antimicrobial therapy remains high-dose co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) for 21 days. A.html: Adjunctive corticosteroids are indicated in hypoxic PCP (PaO2 <9.3 kPa or SaO2 <92% on air). They reduce the treatment-associated inflammatory deterioration and improve survival. This patient's resting hypoxia and profound exertional desaturation meet the threshold.
A.text: Adjunctive corticosteroids are indicated in hypoxic PCP (PaO2 <9.3 kPa or SaO2 <92% on air). They reduce the treatment-associated inflammatory deterioration and improve survival. This patient's resting hypoxia and profound exertional desaturation meet the threshold.

B.html: Ganciclovir targets CMV disease, which can co-exist in advanced HIV but is not the confirmed pathogen here. Immunofluorescence has confirmed Pneumocystis, so antiviral therapy is not the priority additional treatment.
B.text: Ganciclovir targets CMV disease, which can co-exist in advanced HIV but is not the confirmed pathogen here. Immunofluorescence has confirmed Pneumocystis, so antiviral therapy is not the priority additional treatment.

C.html: Nebulised pentamidine is less effective than systemic therapy and is reserved for mild disease or co-trimoxazole intolerance. As monotherapy in a hypoxic patient already on co-trimoxazole it is inappropriate.
C.text: Nebulised pentamidine is less effective than systemic therapy and is reserved for mild disease or co-trimoxazole intolerance. As monotherapy in a hypoxic patient already on co-trimoxazole it is inappropriate.

D.html: ART is essential but is typically deferred about 2 weeks after starting PCP treatment to limit immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, which can worsen respiratory function. Same-day initiation is not the strongest immediate step.
D.text: ART is essential but is typically deferred about 2 weeks after starting PCP treatment to limit immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, which can worsen respiratory function. Same-day initiation is not the strongest immediate step.

E.html: Echinocandins such as caspofungin lack reliable single-agent efficacy against Pneumocystis and are not recommended as standard therapy. Co-trimoxazole remains first-line antimicrobial treatment.

q: A 28-year-old asymptomatic nurse from India, recently employed by an NHS trust, has occupational health screening. She had BCG in childhood. An interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) is positive. Chest radiograph is normal, she has no cough, fever or weight loss, and three sputum samples are not required as she is asymptomatic. She is HIV-negative and not immunosuppressed. According to NICE guidance, which single management option is most appropriate?
options: No treatment; repeat IGRA in 12 months
Isoniazid (with pyridoxine) plus rifampicin for 3 months
Standard quadruple therapy (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) for 6 months
Isolate and start directly observed therapy
explain: A positive IGRA with a normal radiograph and no symptoms indicates latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI), not active disease. 🧫 IGRA measures interferon-gamma released by T-cells sensitised to M. tuberculosis-specific antigens (ESAT-6, CFP-10), which are absent from BCG, so prior vaccination does not cause a false positive (unlike the tuberculin skin test).\n\nNICE recommends treating LTBI in eligible people under 65 to prevent progression to active TB. The recommended regimens are 3 months of isoniazid plus rifampicin, or 6 months of isoniazid alone; pyridoxine is co-prescribed with isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy. Full quadruple therapy is for active disease. Repeat BCG is not indicated and does not treat established infection. Isolation and directly observed therapy apply to infectious active pulmonary TB. Simply repeating the IGRA ignores a treatable latent infection in a healthcare worker.

The recommended regimens are 3 months of isoniazid plus rifampicin, or 6 months of isoniazid alone; pyridoxine is co-prescribed with isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy. Full quadruple therapy is for active disease. Repeat BCG is not indicated and does not treat established infection. Isolation and directly observed therapy apply to infectious active pulmonary TB. Simply repeating the IGRA ignores a treatable latent infection in a healthcare worker.

A.html: Watchful waiting leaves a treatable latent infection untreated in a young healthcare worker at risk of reactivation. NICE advises offering treatment for LTBI in eligible individuals rather than merely monitoring.
A.text: Watchful waiting leaves a treatable latent infection untreated in a young healthcare worker at risk of reactivation. NICE advises offering treatment for LTBI in eligible individuals rather than merely monitoring.

B.html: 3 months of isoniazid plus rifampicin (or 6 months isoniazid) is the NICE-recommended LTBI regimen. Pyridoxine reduces isoniazid-induced neuropathy. This eradicates latent bacilli and prevents progression to active TB.
B.text: 3 months of isoniazid plus rifampicin (or 6 months isoniazid) is the NICE-recommended LTBI regimen. Pyridoxine reduces isoniazid-induced neuropathy. This eradicates latent bacilli and prevents progression to active TB.

C.html: Six-month quadruple therapy is reserved for active tuberculosis. Treating latent infection with the full regimen over-exposes the patient to pyrazinamide and ethambutol toxicity without benefit.
C.text: Six-month quadruple therapy is reserved for active tuberculosis. Treating latent infection with the full regimen over-exposes the patient to pyrazinamide and ethambutol toxicity without benefit.

D.html: BCG does not treat established latent infection and revaccination is not recommended. The relevant intervention is chemoprophylaxis to prevent reactivation.
D.text: BCG does not treat established latent infection and revaccination is not recommended. The relevant intervention is chemoprophylaxis to prevent reactivation.

E.html: Isolation and directly observed therapy target smear-positive infectious active pulmonary TB. This asymptomatic woman with a normal radiograph has latent, non-infectious infection and does not require isolation.

q: A 52-year-old man is treated for smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol. Six weeks into treatment he reports difficulty distinguishing red from green and reduced visual acuity. Fundoscopy is normal. He is otherwise well and adherent. Which single drug is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explain: The combination of reduced visual acuity and impaired red-green colour discrimination with a normal fundus is the classic presentation of ethambutol-induced optic neuritis (retrobulbar neuritis). 👁️ Ethambutol works by inhibiting arabinosyl transferase, blocking arabinogalactan synthesis in the mycobacterial cell wall; its dose-related ocular toxicity affects the papillomacular bundle, producing central scotomas and dyschromatopsia before any visible fundal change.\n\nToxicity is usually reversible if ethambutol is stopped promptly, so patients should have baseline visual acuity/colour vision checked and be warned to report visual symptoms. Isoniazid causes peripheral neuropathy (prevented by pyridoxine) and hepatotoxicity. Rifampicin causes orange secretions, hepatitis and enzyme induction. Pyrazinamide causes hyperuricaemia/gout and hepatotoxicity. Pyridoxine is protective, not toxic. Recognising ethambutol ocular toxicity is a high-yield MRCP fact.

Isoniazid causes peripheral neuropathy (prevented by pyridoxine) and hepatotoxicity. Rifampicin causes orange secretions, hepatitis and enzyme induction. Pyrazinamide causes hyperuricaemia/gout and hepatotoxicity. Pyridoxine is protective, not toxic. Recognising ethambutol ocular toxicity is a high-yield MRCP fact.

A.html: Rifampicin causes orange discolouration of urine, tears and secretions, hepatotoxicity and potent CYP450 enzyme induction. Optic neuritis is not a recognised rifampicin effect.
A.text: Rifampicin causes orange discolouration of urine, tears and secretions, hepatotoxicity and potent CYP450 enzyme induction. Optic neuritis is not a recognised rifampicin effect.

B.html: Isoniazid classically causes peripheral sensory neuropathy (from pyridoxine depletion) and hepatitis. It does not typically produce the central colour-vision loss seen with optic neuritis.
B.text: Isoniazid classically causes peripheral sensory neuropathy (from pyridoxine depletion) and hepatitis. It does not typically produce the central colour-vision loss seen with optic neuritis.

C.html: Pyrazinamide causes hyperuricaemia (may precipitate gout), arthralgia and hepatotoxicity. Visual disturbance is not a feature of pyrazinamide toxicity.
C.text: Pyrazinamide causes hyperuricaemia (may precipitate gout), arthralgia and hepatotoxicity. Visual disturbance is not a feature of pyrazinamide toxicity.

D.html: Ethambutol causes dose-dependent retrobulbar optic neuritis affecting the papillomacular bundle, producing reduced acuity and red-green dyschromatopsia with an initially normal fundus. Stopping the drug promptly usually allows recovery.
D.text: Ethambutol causes dose-dependent retrobulbar optic neuritis affecting the papillomacular bundle, producing reduced acuity and red-green dyschromatopsia with an initially normal fundus. Stopping the drug promptly usually allows recovery.

E.html: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) is co-prescribed with isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy. It is protective and is not a cause of visual toxicity.
E.text: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) is co-prescribed with isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy. It is protective and is not a cause of visual toxicity.

q: A 24-year-old university student is admitted with a 12-hour history of fever, severe headache, photophobia and neck stiffness. He is drowsy with a non-blanching petechial rash on the trunk. Blood pressure is 92/54 mmHg. A lumbar puncture (after a normal CT) shows: opening pressure raised, turbid CSF, white cell count 4200/mm3 (90% neutrophils), protein 2.1 g/L, CSF glucose 1.1 mmol/L with paired serum glucose 5.6 mmol/L, and Gram-negative diplococci on microscopy. Which single feature best explains the low CSF glucose in this condition?
options: Increased glucose consumption by bacteria and activated neutrophils plus impaired glucose transport across inflamed meninges
Osmotic dilution of CSF glucose by raised intracranial pressure
Antibody-mediated destruction of choroid plexus glucose channels
Direct viral cytopathic effect on ependymal cells
explain: This is bacterial (meningococcal) meningitis: turbid CSF, very high neutrophilic pleocytosis, high protein, and markedly low CSF:serum glucose ratio, with Gram-negative diplococci (Neisseria meningitidis). 🧠 The hallmark hypoglycorrhachia arises from two mechanisms: increased glucose utilisation by replicating bacteria and by metabolically activated leucocytes, and impaired facilitated glucose transport across the inflamed blood-brain/meningeal barrier (down-regulated GLUT transporters). A CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.4 strongly favours bacterial infection.\n\nRaised intracranial pressure does not osmotically dilute glucose. Systemic sepsis usually raises blood glucose, and here serum glucose is normal, so the low CSF value reflects intrathecal processes. There is no antibody-mediated channel destruction. Viral meningitis characteristically shows a lymphocytic picture with normal glucose, so a viral cytopathic mechanism is incorrect. Recognising the glucose ratio and its mechanism is central to CSF interpretation.
explainHTML: This is bacterial (meningococcal) meningitis: turbid CSF, very high neutrophilic pleocytosis, high protein, and markedly low CSF:serum glucose ratio, with Gram-negative diplococci (Neisseria meningitidis). 🧠 The hallmark hypoglycorrhachia arises from two mechanisms: increased glucose utilisation by replicating bacteria and by metabolically activated leucocytes, and impaired facilitated glucose transport across the inflamed blood-brain/meningeal barrier (down-regulated GLUT transporters). A CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.4 strongly favours bacterial infection.\n\nRaised intracranial pressure does not osmotically dilute glucose. Systemic sepsis usually raises blood glucose, and here serum glucose is normal, so the low CSF value reflects intrathecal processes. There is no antibody-mediated channel destruction. Viral meningitis characteristically shows a lymphocytic picture with normal glucose, so a viral cytopathic mechanism is incorrect. Recognising the glucose ratio and its mechanism is central to CSF interpretation.

A.html: Bacterial and neutrophil metabolism consumes CSF glucose, while meningeal inflammation impairs facilitated glucose transport into the CSF. Together these produce the low CSF:serum glucose ratio (<0.4) characteristic of bacterial meningitis.
A.text: Bacterial and neutrophil metabolism consumes CSF glucose, while meningeal inflammation impairs facilitated glucose transport into the CSF. Together these produce the low CSF:serum glucose ratio (<0.4) characteristic of bacterial meningitis.

B.html: Raised intracranial pressure reflects inflammation and oedema but does not osmotically dilute glucose. The glucose fall is a metabolic and transport phenomenon, not a dilutional one.
B.text: Raised intracranial pressure reflects inflammation and oedema but does not osmotically dilute glucose. The glucose fall is a metabolic and transport phenomenon, not a dilutional one.

C.html: Sepsis typically raises blood glucose through stress hyperglycaemia, and this patient's serum glucose is normal. Reduced hepatic gluconeogenesis would lower serum, not selectively CSF, glucose.
C.text: Sepsis typically raises blood glucose through stress hyperglycaemia, and this patient's serum glucose is normal. Reduced hepatic gluconeogenesis would lower serum, not selectively CSF, glucose.

D.html: There is no autoantibody-mediated destruction of choroid plexus glucose transporters in acute bacterial meningitis. The mechanism is metabolic consumption and impaired transport, not immune channel injury.
D.text: There is no autoantibody-mediated destruction of choroid plexus glucose transporters in acute bacterial meningitis. The mechanism is metabolic consumption and impaired transport, not immune channel injury.

E.html: Viral meningitis produces a lymphocytic CSF with normal glucose, the opposite of this neutrophilic, low-glucose profile. A viral cytopathic mechanism cannot explain the findings.
E.text: Viral meningitis produces a lymphocytic CSF with normal glucose, the opposite of this neutrophilic, low-glucose profile. A viral cytopathic mechanism cannot explain the findings.

q: A 63-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve (implanted 8 months ago) presents with 3 weeks of low-grade fever, malaise and weight loss. Three sets of blood cultures grow coagulase-negative staphylococci. Transoesophageal echocardiography shows a valve vegetation and a small perivalvular abscess. The isolate is meticillin-resistant. Which single antimicrobial mechanism explains why flucloxacillin would be ineffective against this organism?
options: Production of an extended-spectrum beta-lactamase hydrolysing the beta-lactam ring
Up-regulation of efflux pumps exporting the antibiotic
Acquisition of the mecA gene encoding an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a) with low beta-lactam affinity
Enzymatic modification of the drug by aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes
Porin loss reducing intracellular drug penetration
explain: This is prosthetic valve endocarditis due to meticillin-resistant coagulase-negative staphylococci (a leading cause within the first year of valve surgery). 🦠 Meticillin resistance in staphylococci is mediated by the mecA gene, carried on the SCCmec mobile element, which encodes PBP2a (PBP2'), an alternative penicillin-binding protein with very low affinity for beta-lactams. Because cell-wall transpeptidation can continue via PBP2a even when beta-lactams saturate the normal PBPs, flucloxacillin and other anti-staphylococcal penicillins fail — resistance is target-based, not enzyme-based.\n\nHence beta-lactamase production is not the operative mechanism (flucloxacillin is beta-lactamase-stable anyway). Efflux, aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes and porin loss are resistance strategies in other contexts but do not explain meticillin resistance. Treatment requires a glycopeptide (vancomycin) with rifampicin and gentamicin for prosthetic valve staphylococcal endocarditis, plus surgical assessment for the abscess.
explainHTML: This is prosthetic valve endocarditis due to meticillin-resistant coagulase-negative staphylococci (a leading cause within the first year of valve surgery). 🦠 Meticillin resistance in staphylococci is mediated by the mecA gene, carried on the SCCmec mobile element, which encodes PBP2a (PBP2'), an alternative penicillin-binding protein with very low affinity for beta-lactams. Because cell-wall transpeptidation can continue via PBP2a even when beta-lactams saturate the normal PBPs, flucloxacillin and other anti-staphylococcal penicillins fail — resistance is target-based, not enzyme-based.\n\nHence beta-lactamase production is not the operative mechanism (flucloxacillin is beta-lactamase-stable anyway). Efflux, aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes and porin loss are resistance strategies in other contexts but do not explain meticillin resistance. Treatment requires a glycopeptide (vancomycin) with rifampicin and gentamicin for prosthetic valve staphylococcal endocarditis, plus surgical assessment for the abscess.

A.html: Flucloxacillin is deliberately beta-lactamase-stable, so ESBL production is not the reason it fails against MRSA. ESBLs are relevant to Gram-negative resistance, not staphylococcal meticillin resistance.
A.text: Flucloxacillin is deliberately beta-lactamase-stable, so ESBL production is not the reason it fails against MRSA. ESBLs are relevant to Gram-negative resistance, not staphylococcal meticillin resistance.

B.html: Efflux pumps contribute to resistance in some organisms (e.g. tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones) but are not the mechanism of meticillin resistance in staphylococci.
B.text: Efflux pumps contribute to resistance in some organisms (e.g. tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones) but are not the mechanism of meticillin resistance in staphylococci.

C.html: mecA encodes PBP2a, a transpeptidase with low affinity for beta-lactams. Cell-wall synthesis proceeds despite flucloxacillin binding native PBPs, so all anti-staphylococcal penicillins fail. This target alteration defines meticillin resistance.

D.html: Aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes acetylate, adenylate or phosphorylate aminoglycosides. They have no role in beta-lactam resistance and do not explain flucloxacillin failure.

E.html: Porin loss reduces drug entry in Gram-negative bacteria, but staphylococci lack an outer membrane. Meticillin resistance is due to an altered target (PBP2a), not reduced penetration.

q: A 27-year-old man returns from a 3-week trip to rural Nigeria and presents with cyclical fevers, rigors, headache and jaundice. He did not take chemoprophylaxis. Temperature 39.8C, spleen palpable. Bloods: haemoglobin 92 g/L, platelets 48 x10^9/L, bilirubin 46 micromol/L, creatinine 168 micromol/L. A thick and thin blood film confirms Plasmodium falciparum with 6% parasitaemia. He is drowsy with a lactate of 4.2 mmol/L. Which single management step is most appropriate?
options: Oral artemether-lumefantrine and discharge with review
explain: This is severe/complicated falciparum malaria. 🦟 Features of severity here include impaired consciousness, parasitaemia >2%, jaundice, acute kidney injury (creatinine 168), lactate >2 mmol/L and thrombocytopenia. UK (and WHO) guidance mandates intravenous artesunate as first-line for severe falciparum malaria; it reduces mortality compared with IV quinine (SEAQUAMAT/AQUAMAT trials) by rapidly killing circulating and sequestering parasites across the erythrocytic cycle.\n\nOral therapy is inadequate for severe disease and in a drowsy patient at risk of vomiting. Chloroquine is inappropriate — falciparum in Africa is chloroquine-resistant, and it is not used for severe disease. IV quinine is now second-line where artesunate is available and requires a loading dose plus cardiac/glucose monitoring. Primaquine eradicates hypnozoites of P. vivax/ovale (falciparum has none) and treats gametocytes, so it is not the acute life-saving intervention. Patients should be managed in a high-dependency setting with parasitaemia monitoring.

UK (and WHO) guidance mandates intravenous artesunate as first-line for severe falciparum malaria; it reduces mortality compared with IV quinine (SEAQUAMAT/AQUAMAT trials) by rapidly killing circulating and sequestering parasites across the erythrocytic cycle.\n\nOral therapy is inadequate for severe disease and in a drowsy patient at risk of vomiting. Chloroquine is inappropriate — falciparum in Africa is chloroquine-resistant, and it is not used for severe disease. IV quinine is now second-line where artesunate is available and requires a loading dose plus cardiac/glucose monitoring. Primaquine eradicates hypnozoites of P. vivax/ovale (falciparum has none) and treats gametocytes, so it is not the acute life-saving intervention. Patients should be managed in a high-dependency setting with parasitaemia monitoring.

A.html: Oral artemether-lumefantrine is for uncomplicated malaria. With impaired consciousness, high parasitaemia, AKI and hyperlactataemia this is severe disease requiring parenteral therapy and admission, not discharge.
A.text: Oral artemether-lumefantrine is for uncomplicated malaria. With impaired consciousness, high parasitaemia, AKI and hyperlactataemia this is severe disease requiring parenteral therapy and admission, not discharge.

B.html: IV artesunate is first-line for severe falciparum malaria and lowers mortality versus quinine (SEAQUAMAT/AQUAMAT). It rapidly clears parasites across the erythrocytic cycle. This patient meets multiple severity criteria and needs parenteral treatment.
B.text: IV artesunate is first-line for severe falciparum malaria and lowers mortality versus quinine (SEAQUAMAT/AQUAMAT). It rapidly clears parasites across the erythrocytic cycle. This patient meets multiple severity criteria and needs parenteral treatment.

C.html: African P. falciparum is widely chloroquine-resistant, and chloroquine has no role in severe disease. Using it risks treatment failure and death.
C.text: African P. falciparum is widely chloroquine-resistant, and chloroquine has no role in severe disease. Using it risks treatment failure and death.

D.html: IV quinine is second-line where artesunate is available and, if used, requires a loading dose with cardiac and glucose monitoring. Omitting the loading dose delays therapeutic levels, and artesunate is preferred.
D.text: IV quinine is second-line where artesunate is available and, if used, requires a loading dose with cardiac and glucose monitoring. Omitting the loading dose delays therapeutic levels, and artesunate is preferred.

E.html: Primaquine eradicates the dormant liver hypnozoites of P. vivax and P. ovale, which falciparum does not form. It is not the acute treatment for severe falciparum malaria.
E.text: Primaquine eradicates the dormant liver hypnozoites of P. vivax and P. ovale, which falciparum does not form. It is not the acute treatment for severe falciparum malaria.

q: A 45-year-old woman is admitted with 6 days of profuse watery diarrhoea (up to 10 stools/day), lower abdominal pain and fever. She completed a course of co-amoxiclav for a chest infection 10 days earlier. Examination shows abdominal distension and tenderness. Bloods: white cell count 22 x10^9/L, creatinine 145 micromol/L, albumin 26 g/L, lactate 2.6 mmol/L. Stool testing is positive for Clostridioides difficile toxin. Abdominal radiograph shows colonic dilatation to 7 cm. According to current UK guidance, which single treatment is most appropriate for this severe episode?
options: Oral metronidazole 400 mg three times daily
Oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily
explain: This is severe Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) following broad-spectrum antibiotics. 💊 Severity markers here include WCC >15 x10^9/L, rising creatinine, fever, and evidence of colonic dilatation. Current NICE/UK guidance recommends oral vancomycin (125 mg QDS for 10 days) as first-line for both non-severe and severe CDI; oral fidaxomicin is an alternative, especially to reduce recurrence.\n\nOral vancomycin acts locally in the gut lumen (it is not absorbed) to eradicate C. difficile. Metronidazole is no longer first-line and is reserved for situations where oral vancomycin/fidaxomicin cannot be used. Intravenous vancomycin does not achieve adequate luminal concentrations and is ineffective for CDI (IV metronidazole may be added in life-threatening/ileus cases alongside intracolonic or NG vancomycin). Antimotility agents such as loperamide are contraindicated as they risk toxic megacolon. Rifaximin is not first-line therapy. Surgical review is warranted given colonic dilatation.
explainHTML: This is severe Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) following broad-spectrum antibiotics. 💊 Severity markers here include WCC >15 x10^9/L, rising creatinine, fever, and evidence of colonic dilatation. Current NICE/UK guidance recommends oral vancomycin (125 mg QDS for 10 days) as first-line for both non-severe and severe CDI; oral fidaxomicin is an alternative, especially to reduce recurrence.\n\nOral vancomycin acts locally in the gut lumen (it is not absorbed) to eradicate C. difficile. Metronidazole is no longer first-line and is reserved for situations where oral vancomycin/fidaxomicin cannot be used. Intravenous vancomycin does not achieve adequate luminal concentrations and is ineffective for CDI (IV metronidazole may be added in life-threatening/ileus cases alongside intracolonic or NG vancomycin). Antimotility agents such as loperamide are contraindicated as they risk toxic megacolon. Rifaximin is not first-line therapy. Surgical review is warranted given colonic dilatation.

q: A 19-year-old student presents with 2 weeks of sore throat, fever, marked fatigue and cervical lymphadenopathy. He was prescribed amoxicillin by his GP and then developed a widespread pruritic maculopapular rash. Examination shows exudative tonsillitis, palatal petechiae, symmetrical posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly. Full blood count shows lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes on the film; a monospot test is positive. Which single investigation finding would most specifically confirm recent primary infection with the causative organism?
options: Epstein-Barr viral capsid antigen (VCA) IgG positive with negative IgM
Epstein-Barr viral capsid antigen (VCA) IgM positive with EBNA IgG negative
explain: This is infectious mononucleosis due to primary Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection — classic triad of fever, pharyngitis and lymphadenopathy, with splenomegaly, atypical lymphocytes, and an amoxicillin-induced rash. 🧬 EBV serology dates the infection: VCA IgM positive with EBNA IgG still negative indicates recent/acute primary infection, because anti-EBNA antibodies develop late (typically 6–12 weeks after onset) and persist for life. Their absence therefore excludes past infection and confirms the illness is acute.\n\nEBNA IgG positivity indicates past infection (weeks to months earlier), not acute disease. CMV IgG only indicates prior CMV exposure and does not confirm the EBV diagnosis. VCA IgG with negative IgM suggests remote infection. The heterophile (monospot) test supports the diagnosis but is less specific and can be falsely negative, especially early or in young children; EBV-specific serology is more definitive. Advise avoidance of contact sports for several weeks due to splenic rupture risk.

Their absence therefore excludes past infection and confirms the illness is acute.\n\nEBNA IgG positivity indicates past infection (weeks to months earlier), not acute disease. CMV IgG only indicates prior CMV exposure and does not confirm the EBV diagnosis. VCA IgG with negative IgM suggests remote infection. The heterophile (monospot) test supports the diagnosis but is less specific and can be falsely negative, especially early or in young children; EBV-specific serology is more definitive. Advise avoidance of contact sports for several weeks due to splenic rupture risk.

B.html: CMV IgG merely reflects prior CMV exposure. CMV can cause a mononucleosis-like illness, but a positive IgG does not confirm acute EBV infection in this heterophile-positive patient.

D.html: VCA IgM positivity with absent EBNA IgG is the hallmark of acute primary EBV: IgM appears early and EBNA develops only weeks later. This combination most specifically dates the infection as recent.

q: A 30-year-old healthcare worker sustains a needlestick injury from a hollow-bore needle used on a patient known to be hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) positive with a high viral load. The injured worker completed a full course of hepatitis B vaccination 5 years ago, and their most recent documented anti-HBs titre was 15 mIU/mL (an inadequate/borderline responder). Bloods are taken. Which single post-exposure measure is most appropriate for this worker?
options: No action required as the worker is fully vaccinated
A single hepatitis B vaccine booster dose alone
Hepatitis B immunoglobulin plus a hepatitis B vaccine booster
explain: This is a significant hepatitis B exposure in a known inadequate vaccine responder (anti-HBs <10 mIU/mL is a non-responder; 10–100 is a suboptimal responder). ⚠️ For a high-risk source (HBsAg positive, high viral load) and a worker whose protection is inadequate/uncertain, UK guidance (Green Book) recommends giving both hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) for immediate passive immunity and an accelerated vaccine booster to stimulate an anamnestic active response. HBIG should be given as soon as possible, ideally within 48 hours.\n\n'No action' is unsafe with a borderline titre and high-risk source. A booster alone provides no immediate protection during the window before an anamnestic response, so HBIG is added for a known poor responder facing a high-risk source. Tenofovir/emtricitabine is HIV post-exposure prophylaxis, not hepatitis B PEP in this context. Interferon-alpha treats chronic hepatitis B; it has no role in post-exposure prophylaxis. Baseline and follow-up serology should also be arranged.

A.html: A borderline anti-HBs of 15 mIU/mL indicates suboptimal protection, and the source is high-risk. Doing nothing leaves the worker inadequately protected against a transmissible high-viral-load exposure.

B.html: A booster alone gives no immediate protection during the days before an anamnestic antibody rise. With a poor responder and a high-risk source, passive immunity with HBIG must be added.

C.html: HBIG provides immediate passive protection while the vaccine booster drives an active anamnestic response. This combination is recommended for inadequate responders exposed to a high-risk HBsAg-positive source, given promptly (ideally within 48 hours).

D.html: Tenofovir/emtricitabine is HIV post-exposure prophylaxis. It is not the recommended post-exposure regimen for a hepatitis B exposure, which relies on HBIG and vaccine.
